body.statement: Let \(k,p\in\mathbb N_0\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{k\times p}\).  There is a vector \(\xi^A\) of mutually independent nonconstant two-point, and hence non-Gaussian, sources such that the following holds for every \(q\in\mathbb N_0\), every \(D\in\mathbb R^{k\times q}\), and every vector \(\eta\) of mutually independent nonconstant real sources: if \(\mathcal L(A\xi^A)=\mathcal L(D\eta)\), then there are a surjection \(f:U_A\twoheadrightarrow U_D\) and nonzero scalars \(a_i\), \(i\in U_A\), satisfying \(A_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}\).  Here \(U_A\) and \(U_D\) are the sets of nonzero columns; no location or moment condition is imposed on \(\eta\).
body.proof_tex:
Put \(U=U_A\).  If \(U=\varnothing\), choose arbitrary independent two-point coordinates for \(\xi^A\).  Then \(A\xi^A=0\).  If \(U_D\ne\varnothing\), select \(j_0\in U_D\) and a linear functional \(b^{\mathsf T}\) with \(b^{\mathsf T}D_{:,j_0}\ne0\).  Among the independent scalar variables \((b^{\mathsf T}D_{:,j})\eta_j\), discard those with zero coefficient.  The remaining family is nonempty, mutually independent, and each member is nonconstant, while its sum would be the constant \(b^{\mathsf T}D\eta=0\).  This contradicts \(\text{lem:independent-sum-nondegenerate}\).  Thus \(U_D=\varnothing\), and the empty surjection proves the assertion.  When \(k=0\), both visible sets are empty by definition, so the same conclusion is immediate.

Suppose \(U\ne\varnothing\).  Let \(F\) be the subfield of \(\mathbb R\) generated by the finitely many entries of \(A\); it is countable.  Recursively choose positive numbers \((r_i)_{i\in U}\) algebraically independent over \(F\).  This is possible because at each finite stage the algebraic closure of the countable field already generated is countable, whereas every positive interval is uncountable.  Set
\[
 h_i=r_iA_{:,i},\qquad
 \Lambda=\bigoplus_{i\in U}\mathbb Z h_i.
\]
Indeed, if \(\sum_i m_ih_i=0\) with integers \(m_i\), each coordinate is a polynomial relation \(\sum_i m_iA_{vi}r_i=0\) over \(F\).  Algebraic independence makes every coefficient \(m_iA_{vi}\) zero, and the nonzero column \(A_{:,i}\) then gives \(m_i=0\).  Thus the displayed sum is direct.

Fix \(p_i\in(0,1)\), let the \(Z_i\) be independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities \(p_i\), and put \(\xi_i^A=r_iZ_i\) for \(i\in U\); use arbitrary independent nonconstant two-point laws on the zero columns.  All coordinates are nonconstant and non-Gaussian.  The output law has the \(2^{|U|}\) distinct support points
\[
 \left\{\sum_{i\in U}z_ih_i:z_i\in\{0,1\}\right\},                 \tag{1}
\]
and each point has positive mass.

Suppose this law is also that of \(\sum_{j\in U_D}Y_j\), where \(Y_j=D_{:,j}\eta_j\).  The topological support of a convolution contains the Minkowski sum of the supports of its factors: any neighborhoods of selected support points have positive probabilities, and independence gives positive probability to the sum of those neighborhoods.  Since (1) is finite, fixing one support point of every factor except \(Y_j\) injects \(\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)\), up to translation, into (1).  Hence every \(Y_j\) has finite support.  Each is nonconstant because \(D_{:,j}\ne0\) and \(\eta_j\) is nonconstant.

Choose \(y_j^0\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)\).  For every \(y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)\), the two sums formed by using \(y\) and \(y_j^0\), while fixing support points of all other factors, both belong to (1).  Their difference lies in \(\Lambda\).  Freeness of \(\Lambda\) therefore gives a unique \(\nu_j(y)\in\mathbb Z^U\) such that
\[
 y-y_j^0=\sum_{i\in U}\nu_j(y)_ih_i.
\]
Define the Laurent probability polynomial
\[
 F_j(z)=\sum_{y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)}Pr(Y_j=y)z^{\nu_j(y)}
 \in\mathbb R[z_i^{\pm1}:i\in U].
\]
The sum \(\sum_jy_j^0\) is itself a point of (1), so coefficientwise equality of the two convolution laws and injectivity of the exponent map into \(\Lambda\) give
\[
 \prod_{j\in U_D}F_j(z)
 =z^\gamma\prod_{i\in U}\bigl((1-p_i)+p_iz_i\bigr)                 \tag{2}
\]
for some \(\gamma\in\mathbb Z^U\).

We record the algebra behind the next step.  A field is a unique-factorization domain.  If \(R\) is a unique-factorization domain, write every polynomial in \(R[z]\) as its coefficient content times a primitive polynomial.  Reducing a putative nonprimitive product modulo any prime divisor of all its coefficients shows that the product of two primitive polynomials is primitive.  Factorization over the fraction field, clearing denominators, and this primitive-product fact then give existence and uniqueness of factorization in \(R[z]\).  Induction over \(|U|\) proves that \(\mathbb R[z_i:i\in U]\) is a unique-factorization domain.  Localizing a factorization at the multiplicative set of monomials merely makes the variables into units and retains existence and uniqueness for all other irreducible factors.  Hence the Laurent ring \(\mathbb R[z_i^{\pm1}:i\in U]\) is a unique-factorization domain.

In this Laurent ring, each \((1-p_i)+p_iz_i\) is prime: quotienting by it substitutes the nonzero real value \(-(1-p_i)/p_i\) for \(z_i\) and leaves a Laurent polynomial domain in the other variables.  The factors for distinct \(i\)'s are nonassociated.  Unique factorization in (2) therefore supplies a partition \((I_j)_{j\in U_D}\) of \(U\) such that
\[
 F_j(z)=z^{\gamma_j}\prod_{i\in I_j}\bigl((1-p_i)+p_iz_i\bigr).    \tag{3}
\]
No \(I_j\) is empty, because an empty product in (3) would make \(Y_j\) constant.  If \(i\in I_j\), two support exponents in (3) differing only in coordinate \(i\) show that \(h_i\) is the difference of two support points of \(Y_j\).  Those points lie on \(\mathbb RD_{:,j}\), so \(A_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,j}\) for some \(a_i\ne0\).  Defining \(f(i)=j\) when \(i\in I_j\) gives the required surjection and proportionalities.  The construction used only admissible two-point diagnostic sources and retained the original lattice \(\Lambda\) throughout.
